opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the first three levels, chatbots, reasoners, and agents, are all about doing things humans already know how to do. Even an agent completing a long task is essentially executing within a space that's been defined by human knowledge. There's a correct answer, or at least a clear sense of what "done well" looks like, and we can provide that signal through data or through a reward.

Innovation is different. By definition, you're producing something that isn't in the training distribution. There's no reference answer to imitate, and often you don't even know what the right objective is. If you look at how real scientific breakthroughs happen, a large part of the work is figuring out which question is worth asking. That's very hard to turn into a reward function.

From a reinforcement learning perspective, there's also an exploration problem. Today's RL on large models mostly sharpens what the pretrained model can already do: it raises the probability of good behaviors that were already somewhere in the distribution. True innovation requires exploring regions the model has essentially never seen, over very long horizons, with very sparse and delayed feedback. A researcher might spend months or years on a direction before knowing whether it works. We don't yet have algorithms that explore efficiently under those conditions.

The third issue is verification. For math or code, you can check whether an answer is right. For an innovation, whether a new theory or product or research direction, judging its value is itself extremely hard, and sometimes only becomes clear years later. Without reliable verification, it's hard to build the training loop.

So I'd say the gap isn't just "more capability." It's a qualitative shift from optimizing toward known targets to discovering new targets yourself. That's why I see it as a much bigger jump than the earlier levels. That said, I don't think it's impossible. I think progress on long-horizon agents, better exploration, and having AI work alongside human researchers could gradually get us there.

r001.rationale: The response says the first three levels do things humans already know how to do and operate within a space defined by human knowledge, with a clear sense of what to do well—communicating that they execute within specified tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first three levels—chatbots, reasoners, and agents—share something fundamental: they're all operating within a space that humans have already defined. A chatbot retrieves and recombines what's in the training data. A reasoner works through a problem step by step, but the problem itself, and the tools for solving it, are things we've already written down somewhere. An agent takes actions in the world, but it's executing toward goals we specify, using methods that exist. In all three cases, the model is interpolating within the distribution of human knowledge. It can do that remarkably well, and getting from one level to the next is mostly a matter of scale, better data, and better training signals. Those are hard engineering problems, but they're the same kind of problem.

Innovation is different in kind. Real innovation means producing something that isn't in the distribution—a hypothesis no one has written, a proof technique that didn't exist, a question that nobody thought to ask. And here you run into a very deep issue with how we train these systems. Almost everything we do is imitation at some level. Even reinforcement learning, which people point to as the path beyond imitation, mostly works today because we have a verifier—a math answer is right or wrong, code passes the tests or it doesn't. But the hardest part of innovation is precisely that you don't have a verifier. You don't know in advance what "good" looks like. Einstein didn't have a reward function telling him relativity was correct before he worked it out. So the thing that made RL work for reasoning is exactly the thing that's missing when you try to apply it to genuine discovery.

There's also a question of exploration. Human innovators spend years in a state of productive confusion—reading, trying things, failing, holding contradictory ideas in their heads. Our models are trained to converge quickly to the likely answer. That's great for levels one through three, but it actively works against the kind of open-ended wandering that discovery requires. You'd need a system that can tolerate being wrong for a long time, that can generate its own problems rather than just solving ours, and that has some internal sense of what's interesting even when nothing external is telling it so.

So when I say the gap is large, I don't mean it's impossible. I mean the ingredients that got us here—more data, more compute, more human-labeled signal—don't obviously get us there. We're going to need new ideas about objectives, about self-generated curricula, about how a model evaluates its own novel outputs. And ironically, that itself is an innovation problem that humans still have to solve first.

r001.rationale: The response says the first three levels operate within a space humans have defined: agents pursue goals people specify, and chatbots and reasoners work with existing human knowledge, problems, and methods. It contrasts this with innovation that goes beyond that space.

astra-6.text:
I think the gap is that doing an existing task well and discovering something new are fundamentally different challenges. You can become very good at answering questions, reasoning through problems, and carrying out a sequence of actions while still depending on someone else to define what matters and what success looks like.

Innovation asks you to go beyond that. You have to identify a worthwhile problem, form a hypothesis, and find a way to test it. Often there isn’t a clear answer to compare against. You might spend a long time pursuing an idea before discovering that the premise was wrong. So you need not only reasoning, but also judgment about which direction to explore and how to learn from failure.

And producing something novel isn’t enough. It has to be useful or true. An AI can generate many unusual ideas, but demonstrating that one of those ideas actually advances our understanding is a much higher bar. That loop—from choosing the question to validating a discovery—is why I see innovation as such a large step.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts carrying out tasks with discovering something new, saying AI can execute actions while relying on someone else to define what matters and what success looks like. This communicates the first three levels’ dependence on instructions specifying what to do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big gap is between solving a problem that someone has already defined and figuring out what problem is worth solving in the first place. In many tasks, we can give AI a goal, provide feedback, and measure whether it succeeds. Innovation is much less structured. You may need to question the goal, introduce a new concept, or pursue an idea that initially looks wrong.

And generating something new is only part of it. The system has to recognize which ideas are valuable, test them, learn from failures, and keep going without a clear reward at every step. So even if AI becomes very good at carrying out complex tasks, that doesn’t automatically mean it can make an important discovery. That ability to set a direction and validate genuinely new ideas is why I see innovation as a particularly large jump.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts carrying out tasks with defined goals against innovation, which requires questioning the goal and deciding what problem is worth solving—clearly conveying that the first three levels are limited to executing specified instructions.
